title: Talazoparib and radiation enhance the senolytic efficacy of venetoclax in therapy-induced senescent triple-negative breast cancer cells

sections.abstract:
Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) presents ongoing clinical challenges, often leading to relapse in many patients. The relapse is partly explained by tumor cells transitioning into a senescent state following chemotherapy or radiation, resulting in a more aggressive phenotype, contributing to disease recurrence. Consequently, combining senolytics with traditional treatments could be a viable and promising strategy in treating TNBC. To address this, we induced therapy-induced senescence (TIS) both in vitro and in vivo by combining the poly ADP-ribose polymerase (PARP) inhibitor talazoparib with radiation. We tested whether exposure to the senolytic agent, venetoclax, would result in the eradication of senescent cells and augmentation of apoptosis. TIS Markers, like senescence-associated beta-galactosidase (SA-β-gal), CDKN1A, and senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) marker IL-6, were altered following talazoparib and radiation in both 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 TNBC cell lines. Interestingly, venetoclax treatment following TIS induction led to pronounced apoptotic cell death and significant changes in SA-β-gal and IL-6, implying enhanced sensitivity post-senescence induction. Furthermore, these data were validated in vivo in an immunocompetent TNBC-bearing mouse model, in which venetoclax alone had a modest effect on growth inhibition. However, when combined with radiotherapy/talazoparib, venetoclax dramatically interfered with tumor recovery post-senescence induction, indicating a potential strategy to mitigate disease recurrence. These results suggest that combining radiotherapy with PARP inhibitors with senolytic agents such as venetoclax could potentially overcome disease relapse associated with TNBC.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1007/s44446-025-00034-2.

Keywords: Venetoclax, TNBC, Senescence, PARPi, Radiotherapy (Min.5-Max. 8)
sections.introduction:
Globally, breast cancer ranks as the most frequently diagnosed malignant tumor among women, and it ranks second as the predominant cause of cancer-associated mortality among women (Yedjou, et al. 2017 ; Siegel et al. 2023 ; Dyba et al. 2021 ; Sung et al. 2021 ; Xu et al. 2023 ). A major obstacle to successful management of breast cancer lies in disease relapse, a factor that substantially contributes to elevated mortality rates (Colleoni et al. 2016 ; Ramos and Bentires-Alj 2015 ). Thus, the development of a more potent therapeutic approach aimed at suppressing disease recurrence becomes imperative for improved survival in breast cancer patients. Notably, resistance to commonly used therapies, such as chemotherapy or radiotherapy (Ramos and Bentires-Alj 2015 ; Won and Spruck 2020 ; Yang et al. 2017 ; Alfarouk et al. 2015 ), can lead to the emergence of aggressive variants of tumor cell that may centrally contribute to cancer relapse (Won and Spruck 2020 ; Yang et al. 2017 ; Santos-de-Frutos and Djouder 2021 ; Saleh et al. 2019 ; Gewirtz 2009 ). Consequently, understanding the mechanisms by which cancer cells evade these therapies is crucial for devising more effective strategies to counter cancer relapse.

Senescent cells, a condition characterized by terminal cell cycle arrest that is mostly irreversible while being viable and metabolically active, tend to accumulate during cancer development (Chaib et al. 2022 ). The molecular mechanisms by which cells undergo senescence have been under scrutiny by scientists for multiple decades, pointing to a plethora of causes. These include cancer-causing mutations or activation of oncogenes, impaired functioning of mitochondria, cumulative DNA damage, reactive metabolites, hypoxia or hyperoxia, adverse signals from the extracellular environment, mechanical or shear stresses, infections that overwhelmed the physical state of the cells and substances produced by senescent cells (Martini and Passos 2023 ; Wiley and Campisi 2016 ; Serrano et al. 1997 ; Hernandez-Segura et al. 2018 ; Acosta et al. 2013 ; Yousefzadeh et al. 2021 ). Interestingly, senescence has been shown to have a prominent role in tumor cells response to diverse anticancer therapies, both traditional and targeted, as well as radiotherapy, often referred to as therapy-induced senescence (TIS) (Wang et al. 2020 ; Saleh, et al. 2020 ; Mikula-Pietrasik et al. 2020 ). Moreover, TIS has been observed in breast cancer patients treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy, as evident in several research studies, emphasizing its clinical significance (Saleh et al. 2023 ; Saleh et al. 2021 ; El-Sadoni et al. 2023 ).

Senescent cells can survive exposure to chemotherapy and/or radiation, thereby evading growth arrest and resuming proliferation (Yang et al. 2017 ; Santos-de-Frutos and Djouder 2021 ). Furthermore, senescence has been directly associated with cancer relapse (Demaria et al. 2017 ; Prasanna et al. 2021 ; Yang et al. 2021 ), and the emergence of more aggressive cancer phenotypes (Yang et al. 2017 ; Saleh, et al. 2020 ). Thus, removing or decreasing the impact of senescent tumor cells post-therapy by inducing apoptosis is suggested as a viable and promising approach to enhance therapeutic efficacy of anticancer treatments.

A diverse range of pharmacological compounds, together known as"senolytics,"possess the ability to precisely target and eliminate senescent cells (Yang et al. 2017 ; Chaib et al. 2022 ; Saleh et al. 2020 ; As Sobeai et al. 2022 ; Blasio et al. 2018 ; Zhang 2022 ; Wyles et al. 2022 ). Among these, venetoclax, an inhibitor of BCL-2/BCL-XL/BCL-W, has been reported to be effective in clearing senescent cells, both in cell culture studies and animal models associated with aging-related diseases where senescence plays a role (As Sobeai et al. 2022 ; Velentza et al. 2023 ; Thomalla et al. 2022 ; Stilgenbauer et al. 2016 ; Peris et al. 2023 ; Liu et al. 2023 ; Herling et al. 2018 ; Fan et al. 2023 ). In the context of cancer, venetoclax has been shown to have favorable results, in terms of the ability to eliminate senescent cells, in several tumor cell models triggered into TIS by several agents (Stilgenbauer et al. 2016 ; Uchida et al. 2019 ; Place et al. 2018 ; Zaman et al. 2016 ; Khaw et al. 2016 ; Matulis et al. 2016 ). For instance, venetoclax demonstrates strong senolytic activity in tumor models subjected to doxorubicin (As Sobeai et al. 2022 ). However, there is limited published research on the senolytic potencyl of venetoclax following the development of TIS induced by poly (ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors.

PARP inhibitors (PARPi) have shown promise for management of triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) associated with mutations in BRCA1 and BRCA2 (Anders et al. 2010 ; Anders and Carey 2009 ). While TNBC and other cancers like ovarian cancer may benefit from PARPi, using PARPi alone as monotherapy did not result in significant clinical improvements or an increase in patient survival. Preclinical investigations have demonstrated a synergism when combining PARPi with radiation (Ghorai et al. 2020 ; Chalmers et al. 2010 ; Alotaibi et al. 2016 ), highlighting their role in inducing TIS in cancer cells (Efimova et al. 2010 ). Remarkably, TIS induced by combination of PARPi and radiation has been linked to aggressive cancer recurrence, as senescent cells tend to be unstable and evade growth arrest, allowing tumor proliferation. This phenomenon is hypothesized to significantly lead to therapeutic failure and subsequent relapse (Gewirtz et al. 2016 ).

This study employed two TNBC cell lines to investigate venetoclax's capacity, alone or in combination with PARPi and radiation, to selectively eliminate senescent breast tumor cells after they underwent TIS. These in vitro findings were corroborated in an immunocompetent mouse model, which provides a valid model to study the intricate cellular interaction between the immune system and cellular senescence in relation to tumor development (Paffenholz, et al. 2022 ). The findings from this research contribute additional evidence supporting the efficacy of senolytics in eliminating senescent tumor cells post-exposure to anticancer treatment.
sections.methods:
MDA-MB231 TNBC cancer cells and 4T1 murine mammary carcinoma cells were obtained in cryogenic tubes from the American Type Culture Collection (ATCC) and were kept at −150°C. The cells were grown in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, cat# 11–965-092) with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS) and 1% penicillin/streptomycin antibiotics from Gibco (cat# 15,140,122, Waltham, MA, USA). Talazoparib (cat#S7048) and venetoclax (cat#GDC-0199) were acquired from Selleckchem (Houston, TX, USA). Dimethyl sulfoxide (DMSO, cat# sc-358801) was used to dissolve chemicals, ensuring the maximum final concentration did not exceed 0.1%, and delivered in dark at desired volume to attain desirable concentration. TIS was established in the cell lines by pre-treating them with talazoparib (1 µM) for 3 h followed by 6 Gy radiation for an additional 24 h. The media containing talazoparib was washed away and further incubation for 48 h was executed. After 72 h post-radiation, venetoclax (10 µM) was added and incubated for an another 24 h.

mRNA was obtained from 4T1 and MDA-MB-231 TNBC cell lines through RNeasy mini kit (cat# 74,104, Qiagen, Hilden, Germany) as per manufacturer’s guide. 2 μg of mRNA was reverse transcribed to cDNA using a high-capacity cDNA reverse transcription kit (cat# RT31-020 Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The conditions for the conversion of mRNA to cDNA were 25 °C for 10 min, 37 °C for 120 min, then 85 °C for 5 min using a thermocycler, and the cDNA was stored at − 20 °C until used. The qPCR setting was as follows: 40 cycles of three thermal steps i.e., 50 °C for 2 min, 95 °C for 10 min, then 95 °C for 15 s, with subsequent 60 °C for another one minute. For quantification purposes, GAPDH was used as a reference gene. Three replicates were executed for every 200 ng sample. qPCR was used to measure the apoptotic expression and senescence-related genes including TP53, CDKN1A, IL-6, and CASP3 (Joyce and Quantitative 2002 ).

The primers used in this study were obtained from ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA) and the primer that were used are: TP53 (tumor suppressor phosphoprotein) (IDs Hs01034249_m1, Mm01731290_g1), CDKN1A (cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitor) (IDs Hs00355782_m1, Mm00432448_m1), IL-6 (Interleukin-6) (IDs Hs00174131_m1, Mm00446190_m1), (Cysteine-aspartic acid protease) (IDs Hs00234387_m1, Mm01195085_m1), and GAPDH (glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase) (IDs Hs02786624_g1, Mm99999915_g1). Primers were obtained from ThermoFisher Scientific (Waltham, MA, USA). ΔΔCT method was utilized for quantifying relative gene expression. All results were expressed as means ± standard errors.

Senescence in immunocompetent mice was confirmed using histochemical staining for SA-β-galactosidase (SA-β-gal) and C12-FDG (cat# D2893 Waltham, MA, USA), a SA-β-gal substrate, following established protocols (Marzullo et al. 2022 ). For the SA-β-gal assay, incubation was performed overnight at 37 °C in a CO 2 -free incubator with X-gal substrate in a staining buffer at pH 6.0. After washing with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), cells were examined with bright-field microscopy. Senescent cells showed intense blue staining in comparison to non-senescent cells, with distinct morphological features. To detect C12-FDG, a fluorescence-based method was employed. Cellular pH was artificially raised to 6 using bafilomycin A1 (100 nM) to inhibit lysosome function for 60 min. Subsequently, cells were exposed to 33 µM of C12-FDG, which is cut by β-galactosidase to emit fluorescence. Flow cytometry was then performed to identify and measure the fluorescent signal, with senescent cells expected to exhibit high C12-FDG positivity, while non-senescent cells were C12-FDG negative.

The Annexin V/PI assay (cat# 640,934, BioLegend, San Diego, CA, USA) was utilized to detect and assess apoptosis in the experimentally treated groups(Dong et al. 2009 ). The assay was carried out as per ‏ manufacturer’s recommendation. Briefly, after apoptosis induction, the cells were washed with PBS and treated with trypsin to detach them, followed by centrifugation. The cell pellet was placed again in 500 μL of Annexin V binding buffer which contained 5 μL of annexin V-FITC and 5 μL of 7-AAD and grown at room temperature for 15 min, protected from light. Flow cytometry was utilized to quantify Annexin V-FITC and PI signals. Four cell sub-populations were witnessed: non-apoptotic (Annexin V-negative/7-AAD -negative), early apoptotic (Annexin V-positive/7-AAD -negative), late apoptotic (Annexin V-positive/7-AAD -positive), and necrotic (Annexin V-negative/7-AAD -positive). The apoptosis calculations involved percentages of both early and late apoptotic cells (Alotaibi et al. 2016 ).

All BALB/c female mice were in-house and bred at Animal Biological Service Unit at School of Pharmacy, King Saud University (KSU).. Animal handling complied with the Ethics Committee of the KSU and approved by the Deanship for Scientific Research at KSU. Female mice aged 5 to 6 weeks were kept under pathogen-free environment offered. First, 4T1 cells were cultured in a 75 cm 2 flask at 37 °C under humid with 5% CO 2 . Cells were then subjected to talazoparib and radiation in vitro to trigger senescence. Next, harvesting was performed as per standard cell culture procedure. In PBS-Matrigel (1:1 dilution), 1 million cells were suspended and inoculated subcutaneously into the rear flank for each cohort (untreated and radiation plus talazoparib). Tumor growth was observed routinely. Treatment was started once average tumor volume was about 150 to 200 mm 3 . Afterwards, the senolytic agent, venetoclax, was delivered at 100 mg/kg through oral gavage on alternate days for three doses, and tumor volume was estimated using a Vernier caliper. Lastly, tumor cells were drawn for subsequent studies.

Haematoxylin and eosin (H&E) (cat# ab245880) staining was used to assess tissue structure and integrity on tumor samples following a protocol published previously (Softah, et al. 2023 ). Briefly, the tumors were separated and immersed in formalin (10%) for 7 days to undergo fixation. After that, the samples underwent dehydration, clearing, infiltration, and were subsequently embedded in paraffin wax. The paraffin blocks were then cut into 6 µm sections and dried at temperatures exceeding 65 °C. These sections were stained and observed with H&E stain and light microscope (Nikon, Tokyo, Japan), respectively, at 400 × magnification. Image analysis was employed using ImageJ 1.54g (Bethesda, MA, USA) to quantify degraded cells, with 10 images analyzed per cohort.

The DNA fragmentation was investigated with terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase-mediated dUTP nick-end labeling (TUNEL) staining, which is considered a marker for apoptosis (Loo and TUNEL assay. 2002 ) The TUNEL Assay Kit—BrdU-Red (cat# ab66110) was obtained from Abcam (Cambridge, UK). The assay was conducted as per company's instructions. The tumor samples were fixed with formaldehyde, washed, and treated with proteinase K solution, and further incubated for 5 min at 25 C°. The tissues were refixed and rinsed for a second time. Next, incubation in DNA labelling solution for 1 h at 37 °C was performed. Another washing was performed, followed by incubation in the antibody solution for 30 min at 25°C. Finally, 7-AAD/RNase A solution was added, and the tissues were incubated for 30 min at 25°C. Fluorescence microscopy was utilized to review observe and quantify the fluorescence intensity, where positive nuclei were calculated as a percentage (%) of total nuclei.

To determine differences among groups, one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted, followed by a post hoc Tukey’s test. Statistical significance was set at p-value was less than 0.05. All the statistical analyses were executed through GraphPad Prism 10 software Inc. (San Diego, CA, USA).
sections.results:
Initially, we ran preliminary experiments to choose an appropriate PARPi. Studies indicated that PARPi play a significant role in combating cancer (Javle and Curtin 2011 ). Two PARPi were chosen: talazoparib and niraparib (1uM). As demonstrated in Fig. 1 , both talazoparib and niraparib combined with radiation significantly increase the senescence surrogate, C12-FDG, in both MDA-MB231 and 4T1 cell lines. However, the fluorescence intensity of talazoparib combined with radiation showed distinctly higher fluorescence intensity. Consequently, talazoparib was chosen for all subsequent experiments.

Induction of senescence by PARP inhibitors and radiation. MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cell lines were treated with drug-free control (black), 6 Gy gamma radiation (Rad) (red), 1 µm talazoparib (TLZ) (blue), 1.4 µm niraparib (NRP) (purple), Rad and TLZ (Rad + TLZ) (vivid brown), or Rad and NRP (Rad + NRP) (green). C 12 FDG expressing (senescent) cell subpopulations were quantified using a flow cytometry-based assay. ( a ) Representative flow cytometry charts of senescent MDA-MB-231 cells stained with C 12 FDG. The x-axis represents the intensity of cells stained with C 12 FDG that underwent cellular senescence. ( b ) The quantification of senescent populations in the experimental groups in MDA-MB-231. A significant increase of C 12 FDG positive cells was observed in TLZ, Rad + TLZ, and Rad + NRP treated cells compared to control, while no significant change was seen in other groups relative to control. 4T1. ( c ) Representative flow cytometry charts of senescent 4T1 cells stained with C 12 FDG. ( d ) The quantification of senescent populations in the experimental groups in 4T1. A significant increase of C 12 FDG positive cells was observed in Rad + TLZ and Rad + NRP treated cells compared to control, while no significant change was seen in other groups relative to control. Rad + TLZ significantly induced the highest senescent subpopulations in both cell lines. Values represent means ± standard error of means (SEM) of three independent experiments. ns; non-significant, *; P < 0.05, ****; P < 0.0001 based on one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's honest significance post-hoc test

The association between exposure to venetoclax and sensitizing tumor cells to chemotherapy has been documented in several studies (Numan, et al. 2018 ; Richard-Carpentier et al. 2020 ; Wang, et al. 2020 ). In our study, venetoclax (10 µM) did not demonstrate notable apoptosis induction in MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells (Fig. 2 ). However, administering venetoclax subsequent to combining PARPi and radiation synergistically induced apoptotic cell death in both cell types (Fig. 2 ).

Impact of venetoclax on apoptosis in radiation/talazopairb-induced senescent cancer cells. MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells were treated with drug-free control (black), 10 µm venetoclax (Ven) (purple), the combination of radiation and talazoparib (Rad + TLZ) (vivid brown), or the combination of Rad, TLZ, and Ven (Rad + TLZ + Ven) (green). ( a ) Representative flow cytometry charts of apoptosis of MDA-MB-231 cells stained with Annexin V and 7-AAD. The x-axis represents the intensity of cells stained with Annexin V that underwent apoptosis, while the Y-axis represents the intensity of cells stained with 7-AAD, which indicates necrosis. ( b ) The quantification of apoptotic populations in the experimental groups in MDA-MB-231. Venetoclax significantly shifted cells to apoptosis in radiation/talazoparib -induced senescent cells relative to other experimental groups. ( c ) Representative flow cytometry charts of apoptosis of the experimental groups in 4T1. ( d ) The quantification of apoptotic populations in the experimental groups in 4T1. Venetoclax significantly promoted apoptosis after the induction of senescence by radiation and talazoparib relative to other experimental groups. Values represent means ± standard error of means (SEM) of three independent experiments. *; P < 0.05, ****; P < 0.0001 based on one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's honest significance post-hoc test

Next, we investigated the impact of venetoclax on breast tumor cells undergoing TIS due to combined radiation and PARP inhibition. We conducted qRT-PCR experiments to assess expressional changes in genes linked with TIS and apoptosis. Specifically, we looked at three established senescence markers (TP53, CDKN1A, and IL-6), along with caspase 3 (CASP3) as an indicator of apoptosis. These studies suggested that radiation plus PARPi considerably elevated the expression of all genes, excluding CDKN1A on 4T1 cell line, within 72 h post-treatment relative to control (Fig. 3 ). Moreover, a 24-h treatment with venetoclax after radiation + PARPi reduced the senescence-associated secretory phenotype (SASP) levels, as revealed by IL-6 levels. Also, we found that p53 gene expression upregulation was suggestively decreased when venetoclax was added, which signifies that cells undergo extreme genotoxicity and cellular stress post-venetoclax therapy (Fig. 3 a). In addition, expression levels of caspase-3 and p21, markers of apoptosis and senescence, respectively, were assessed. Exposure to venetoclax following radiation and PARPi led to a vigorous increase in caspase-3 expression, with nominal effect on p21 levels (no enhancement of senescence) in the 4T1 cell line, as shown in Fig. 3 b & 3d. Collectively, our findings support that the function of venetoclax in a murine cell line (4T1 as a senolytic in this model) is likely to be mediated through suppression of senescence genes and overexpression of apoptosis genes (Fig. 3 b & 3 d).

Effect of venetoclax on senescence and apoptosis-associated genes in radiation/talazopairb-induced 4T1 senescent cells. cells were treated with drug-free control (black), 10 µm venetoclax (Ven) (blue), the combination of 6 Gy gamma Radiation and 1 µm talazoparib (Rad + TLZ) (Rad) (red), or the combination of Rad, TLZ, and Ven (Rad + TLZ + Ven) (green). ( a ) TP53 was significantly downregulated in cells treated with venetoclax after the induction of senescence by the combination therapy of radiation and talazoparib compared with other group. ( b ) no changed was observed in CDKN1A expression level in Rad + TLZ + Ven group relative to Rad + TLZ group. ( c ) IL6 was significantly inhibited in cells treated with Rad + TLZ + Ven relative to cells treated with Ven or Rad + TLZ. ( d ) CASP3 was significantly upregulated in cells exposed to Rad + TLZ + Ven compared to other groups. Gene expression was quantified using RT-PCR. Values represent means ± sstandard error of means (SEM) of three independent experiments. ns; non-significant, *; P < 0.05, **; P < 0.01, ***; P < 0.001, and ****; P < 0.0001 based on one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's honest significance post-hoc test

The previously presented in vitro data indicate that pre-treatment of irradiated breast tumor cells with a PARPi robustly induces senescence, and the subsequent treatment with venetoclax (a senolytic) promoted apoptosis. To validate these results in vivo, 4T1 murine breast cancer cells were first exposed to talazoparib, followed by irradiation (6Gy), and given 72 h to undergo senescence, reaching approximately 80% senescent cells. Irradiated cells treated with talazoparib, and non-irradiated cells (deprived of talazoparib were inserted into the flanks of BALB/C mice. The tumor cells were then allowed to nurture till they became palpable on day 4 post-implantation.

Venetoclax was administered orally at a dosage of 10 mg/kg for three doses, given on every alternate day on days 5, 7, and 9. Figure 5 A shows that both radiation + talazoparib and venetoclax alone temporarily suppressed tumor growth. However, the most prominent impact was seen when venetoclax was given following radiation and talazoparib, leading to a decrease in tumor volume (shrinkage) without any subsequent recovery throughout the study duration.

Additional investigations were conducted to examine the results depicted in Fig. 4 a. By assessing the histopathological markers of the tumor samples using H&E staining, we observed that untreated (control) tumors showed pleomorphic shapes and open chromatin. Also, blood vessels were seen (angiogenesis) for more supply of oxygen and nutrients, tumor cells in the nude were mixed with inflammatory cells, and the destructive tumor cells accounted for approximately 2% according to Evan’s grade (Fig. 4 b). Furthermore, tumor samples exposed to radiation and PARPi exhibited degenerated tumor cells, resulting in tissue loss and necrotic areas with hemorrhage (Fig. 4 b), destruction of cells reached 40% and graded IIa. Tumor samples subjected to venetoclax alone displayed mild destruction of tumor cells around 22% and were graded IIa (Fig. 4 b). In agreement with the tumor decline demonstrated in Fig. 4 a, tumor cells subjected to PARPi (talazoparib) plus radiation followed by venetoclax showed some destruction of tumor cells which replaced by stroma, inflammatory cells and necrotic debris (Fig. 4 b), and destruction of tumor cells was 43% and graded IIb (Table 1 ).

Assessment of senolytic effect of venetoclax in 4T1-dervied in vivo tumors following radiation and talazoparib. 4T1 cells were exposed to 6 Gy following 1 μM Talazoparib at in vitro settings to induce senescence, then cells were implanted into Balb/c mice. The mice in group Ven (blue) and Rad + TLZ + Ven (green) were treated with venetoclax 100 mg/kg (p.o.) with 3 doses on day 1,3,5 after tumor reached 200–300 cm. 3 . ( a ) Quantification of tumor volume expressed as percentage of tumor volume relative to the average of tumor volume within each group at Day 0 within each group. Tumor growth was significantly stalled in Rad + TLZ + Ven compared to other groups on day 6 and 8. Values represent means ± standard error of means (SEM). **p < 0.01, indicate statistical significance among treatment groups (one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey's post hoc test; n = 6 mice). ( b ) Histopathological screening of tumor samples using H&E staining (H&E-400x) in Control (I), Ven (II), Rad + TLZ (III), and Rad + TLZ + Ven (IV). Green arrows indicate condensed aggregations of tumor cells. N; necrotic areas and S; stroma. ( c ) Representative TUNEL assay images illustrating apoptotic tumor cells in Control (I), Ven (II), Rad + TLZ (III), and Rad + TLZ + Ven (IV)

Viable cells count of tumor, destruction % and Evan’s grade in untreated and treated tumors

Data = mean ± SEM, p ≤ 0.05 considered significant

*a significant against untreated control

*b significant against RT

Following the histopathological studies, the TUNEL assay was employed to analyze the DNA fragmentation and nuclear rupture. The results depicted in Fig. 4 c reveal that tumor cells in the untreated group exhibit a round and intact appearance, highlighting the absence of apoptosis. The tumor cells subjected to the triple treatment of PARPi plus radiation followed by venetoclax displayed evident DNA fragmentation and nuclear rupture, demonstrating that these senescent cells were highly prone to apoptotic cell death triggered by venetoclax. Conversely, both groups of tumors treated with either PARPi plus radiation or venetoclax alone exhibited minimal DNA fragmentation and reduced signs of apoptosis in contrast to the triple regimen. Overall, the maximum senolytic effect of venetoclax is observed when tumor cells are exposed to PARPi -irradiated tumors, whereas its impact on non-irradiated tumor cells resulted in minimal tumor shrinkage.
sections.discussion:
There is no doubt that cancer recurrence remains an intractable problem in the treatment of TNBC, despite the tangible progress made in personalized therapy. TNBC patients have a higher chance of relapse compared to other breast cancer types, and TIS is presumed to be a predominant contributor to disease relapse (Schmid et al. 2020 ). The selective eradication of senescent cancer cells by shifting them to an irreversible programmed cell death, stat-apoptosis, could be a viable and effective option to overcome the ramifications of TIS. To this end, we previously demonstrated a proof of concept with a “two-punch” method in which we experimentally induced TIS using a PARPi and radiation combination, followed by a senolytic agent, navitoclax, resulting in the successful induction of apoptosis and removal of senescent cells in a TNBC cellular model, and in vivo immunocompetent mice (Softah, et al. 2023 ). In this study, we substantiate this concept with another FDA-approved senolytic agent, venetoclax, paving the way for possible solutions for treatment failure in TNBC.

Initially, we sought to determine a suitable PARPi that induces senescence in synergism with radiation in MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cell lines. While both talazoparib and niraparib combined with radiation resulted in TIS, a more profound induction of senescence was observed with talazoparib and radiation combination. While the enzymatic inhibition ability of both is the same, the PARP trapping potency of talazoparib is reported to be much higher than that of niraparib (100-fold greater), which could partially explain the results reported here (Dong et al. 2009 ). This aligns with reports of talazoparib's greater potency across cancer types, including our observations in TNBC models. Interestingly, both PARPi have been shown to have interindividual differences in their effects on different melanoma cells, highlighting the importance of drug-specific rather than class-wide responses(Weigert et al. 2020 ; Huart, et al. 2022 ).

Following senescence induction utilizing the combined treatment of talazoparib and radiation, we next tested the ability of venetoclax, a selective BCL-2 inhibitor, to eliminate senescent TNBC cells selectively. Treatment of senescent MDA-MB-231 and 4T1 cells with venetoclax resulted in a significant reduction in viability, with minimal impact on non-senescent control cells, which remained largely unaffected. This observation aligns with the hypothesis that senescent cells develop a dependency on anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-2, rendering them particularly vulnerable to BCL-2 inhibition(Ou et al. 2021 ). We and others have shown that the combination of a PARPi (talazoparib or olaparib) and radiation, followed by the senolytic agent, navitoclax, resulted in apoptosis induction and eradication of senescent cells in several tumor cell lines, including MDA-MB-231, 4T1, and A549 adenocarcinomic human alveolar basal epithelial cells (Softah, et al. 2023 ; Weigert et al. 2020 ). Interestingly, the senolytic activity achieved with navitoclax was greater than with venetoclax. This observation has been noted by several studies (Leverson, et al. 2015 ). This effect may be attributed to navitoclax’s molecular mechanism of action, which target multiple anti-apoptotic proteins, BCL-2, BCL-XL, BCL-W, and BCL-B, while venetoclax is a selective BCL-2 inhibitor, as supported by several studies. Venetoclax (ABT-199) has a satisfactory safety profile and is approved for management of both first-line and relapsed/refractory chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) and acute myeloid leukemia (AML) (Khaw et al. 2016 ).

Looking at the impact of venetoclax combined with PARPi and radiation therapy on apoptosis and senescence-related genes revealed intriguing observations. First, the addition of venetoclax after radiation + PARPi resulted in the upregulation of caspase-3, while the p53 gene was significantly downregulated. The p53 gene is known to be mutated in the 4T1 cell line, which could partially explain the inconsistencies in response to venetoclax with the PARPi and radiation combination (Berglind et al. 2008 ; Schrors et al. 2020 ). The p 53 gene’s role in regulating apoptosis and senescence is well documented, and its downregulation may reflect an alternative, p53-independent pathway of venetoclax-mediated cell death. Second, IL-6 mRNA expression, which is vital in inflammatory responses and is a component of SASP, was also significantly reduced after the addition of venetoclax. Whether this decrease in IL-6 results directly from BCL-2 inhibition or reflects effective senolytic activity remains to be elucidated. Several reports have delineated the intricate relationship between the BCL-2 protein and inflammatory cytokines, including IL-6. For instance, Diamantidis and colleagues described a feedback mechanism in multiple myeloma, wherein the bone marrow microenvironment induces IL-6 production by myeloid cells, which in turn activates a survival loop that upregulates anti-apoptotic proteins such as BCL-2, BCL-XL, and MCL-1. Venetoclax, by selectively inhibiting BCL-2, disrupts this feedback loop and promotes apoptosis(Wang, et al. 2020 ; Diamantidis et al. 2022 ; Moser-Katz et al. 2020 ). These findings align with previous reports underscoring the crucial role of IL-6 in cellular senescence and tumor microenvironment modulation (Acosta et al. 2013 ; Freund et al. 2011 ; Kojima et al. 2013 ; Ortiz-Montero et al. 2017 ; Mosteiro, et al. 2018 ).The downregulation of IL-6 in our model is consistent with the notion that venetoclax combined with radiation + PARPi has favorable senolytic activity.

Next, we sought to validate the data in vivo in an immunocompetent mouse model. While venetoclax alone demonstrated modest antitumor activity, the maximum tumor inhibitory effect was observed in the implanted 4T1 cells exposed to PARPi and radiation then subsequently exposed to venetoclax . Herein, the results are in line with our previous findings using another senolytic agent, navitoclax, although the dose used for venetoclax was 100 mg/kg, whereas the navitoclax dose was 50 mg/kg (Softah, et al. 2023 ). Notably, the radiation dose used here was relatively low compared to other studies (Saleh et al. 2020 ). This may represent a clinically favorable balance between antitumor efficacy and minimized toxicity, potentially minimizing radiation-associated adverse effects. The histopathological and TUNEL analyses revealed extensive apoptosis and necrosis in the triple-therapy group, accompanied by stromal remodeling and immune infiltration, suggesting modulation of the immune system and changes in the tumor microenvironment. Resistance to venetoclax, resulting from the upregulation of anti-apoptotic proteins and dysfunctional signaling pathways relevant to cell survival mechanisms, is a major factor contributing to venetoclax resistance (Yue et al. 2020 ). The finding presented here show that preconditioning the tumor microenvironment by radiation and PARPi prior to venetoclax treatment could be a viable and effective strategy to overcome resistance and prevent relapse in TNBC.

There is emerging evidence indicating that chemotherapy- or radiotherapy-induced senescence is indeed associated with cancer relapse, which has significant socioeconomic ramifications. Senescent cells can contribute to chemotherapy or radiotherapy resistance, promote metastasis, and alter the tumor microenvironment. For example, a report by Acklin and others showed that doxorubicin-associated cardiotoxicity and cisplatin-associated peripheral neuropathy were exacerbated by TIS (Acklin et al. 2020 ; Lerida-Viso et al. 2022 ). Consequently, senolytic drugs have emerged as a viable option to mitigate the impact of TIS on cancer recurrence. Interestingly, the precise pathomechanism driving TIS remains a matter of conjecture. However, cell culture studies and animal models speculate that impairment in DNA damage response, oncogene-induced senescence (OIS), telomere dysfunction, oxidative stress and mitochondrial dysfunction, epigenetic alterations, and cell cycle arrest could be driving causes of TIS in cancer recurrence (Zhu et al. 2020 ; Schumacher et al. 2021 ; Crouch 2022 ; Rossiello et al. 2022 ). The use of venetoclax has not only been shown to reduce TIS but also allows radiation to be used at a lower dose. This can result in fewer adverse events associated with radiation. In contrast to previous reports, venetoclax has the advantage of not impacting platelets, improving overall treatment tolerability.

Several studies have demonstrated the effectiveness of triple combination therapy, which encompasses radiation, a PARPi, and senolytics, as seen in the results presented here(Huart, et al. 2022 ; Fujimoto et al. 2022 ). The reduction in IL-6 expression and changes in immune cell infiltration throughout the tumor microenvironment suggest that immune-mediated mechanisms may play a role in eliminating TIS. Therefore, combining senolytic therapies with immunotherapies, such as immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), may yield synergistic therapeutic effects. For instance, a handful of clinical trials are currently evaluating combination of programmed cell death-1 (PD-1) inhibitors and radiation therapy for TNBC, with promising preliminary results (Quintana et al. 2024 ). It would be interesting to investigate whether adding senolytics to such regimens enhances anti-tumor efficacy. Senescent cells have been reported to overexpress PD-1 protein, which might indicate that PD-1 inhibitors may indirectly possess senolytic properties by enhancing immune-mediated clearance of senescent cells.
sections.conclusion: The data presented here demonstrate the beneficial impact of adding venetoclax as a senolytic drug post-PARP inhibition and radiation therapy. This regimen was effective in inducing apoptosis and eliminating senescent TNBC cells. Moreover, the in vitro data were further corroborated in an immunocompetent mouse model bearing TNBC tumors. Consequently, this study substantiates the use of venetoclax to mitigate the TIS impact on cancer recurrence and could potentially be a promising therapeutic approach for enhancing treatment success in TNBC.
